name: Proof of Stake
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Skin in the Game: How Proof of Stake Replaces Work With Wealth
lesson.summary: Proof of stake is a consensus mechanism that secures a blockchain by requiring validators to lock up the network's own token as collateral rather than by requiring them to burn electricity on computational puzzles, substituting an economic penalty for a physical one.
lesson.body:
A consensus mechanism, in general, is a set of rules that lets a network of independent, mutually distrusting nodes agree on a single, valid history of transactions. Proof of work solves this by making agreement expensive to fake, since rewriting history would require redoing an enormous amount of computation. Proof of stake solves the same underlying problem a different way. Instead of nodes competing to solve a computational puzzle, a set of validators is selected, often through a semi-random process weighted by how much of the network's token each one has staked, to propose and confirm blocks.

The mechanics center on collateral. A validator locks up a stake, a deposit of the network's own token, as a bond. If the validator behaves correctly, proposing valid blocks and correctly confirming others, it earns rewards, typically a mix of newly issued tokens and transaction fees, much like a mining reward but without the energy cost. If a validator behaves dishonestly, for example by signing two conflicting blocks at the same height, or by being offline and unavailable for an extended period, the protocol can destroy some or all of its staked tokens, a penalty called slashing. This is the sense in which proof of stake gives validators skin in the game, their own capital is directly at risk if they misbehave, in the same way a miner's sunk cost in hardware and electricity is at risk in proof of work, just denominated differently.

The clearest real world example is Ethereum. In September 2022, in an upgrade widely referred to as the Merge, Ethereum switched its entire consensus layer from proof of work to proof of stake. Running a full validator on Ethereum requires staking 32 ETH. The Ethereum Foundation and independent researchers have estimated that this change cut the network's energy consumption by more than ninety nine percent, since validating blocks no longer requires competing banks of specialized mining hardware running continuously.

That efficiency gain comes with trade offs. Proof of stake systems have faced a theoretical concern called nothing at stake, the worry that, unlike in proof of work where computing power cannot be duplicated across competing chains without duplicating cost, a validator in some naive stake based designs could cheaply validate multiple competing chain histories at once, since signing does not consume a physical resource the way hashing does. Modern implementations, including Ethereum's, address this directly through slashing rules that punish exactly this kind of double signing. A separate and more practical worry is capital concentration, since running a validator requires a meaningful token stake, and many ordinary holders instead delegate their tokens to staking pools or centralized exchanges, which can concentrate influence over block production among a smaller number of large operators than proof of work's more geographically dispersed hardware investment tends to produce.

Because a validator's stake is denominated in the network's own token, proof of stake ties a blockchain's security directly to the market value of that token, a feedback loop that does not exist in proof of work, where security depends instead on the separate markets for computing hardware and electricity.
